questions.question: When driving a tractor-trailer with ABS, what should you do?

options.text: Use extra braking force to activate the ABS.
Use less braking pressure than normal.

questions.correctAnswerText: Brake normally.
questions.explanation: When you have ABS, brake the same way you would in a vehicle without ABS.

questions.question: What does the emergency air line do?

options.text: It is controlled by the foot brake.
It is connected to the relay valves.
It supplies air to the trailer air tanks.

questions.correctAnswerText: It supplies air to the trailer air tanks.
questions.explanation: The emergency air line supplies air to trailer air tanks and controls the emergency brakes.

questions.question: What happens if you use the trailer hand brake during a jackknife?
questions.correctAnswerText: It continues the skid.
questions.explanation: Using the trailer hand brake during a skid makes the skid worse. Release the brakes to help your tires grip the road again.

questions.question: Why do combination vehicles need more road space than other commercial vehicles?

options.text: They need more space to turn and stop.

questions.correctAnswerText: They need more space to turn and stop.
questions.explanation: Combination vehicles are longer and need more space to turn and stop. Managing space properly is very important when driving them.

questions.question: When is a trailer most likely to swing around?

options.text: When traveling in a straight line.

questions.correctAnswerText: When it is empty.
questions.explanation: An empty trailer takes longer to stop and is most likely to swing out and hit other vehicles. A lightly loaded or empty trailer is more prone to this.

questions.question: Which vehicle is most likely to experience the "crack-the-whip" effect?
questions.correctAnswerText: A triple combination
questions.explanation: Double and triple combinations are most at risk of rolling over from the "crack-the-whip" effect.

questions.question: How do you test the trailer service brakes?

options.text: Move forward slowly and press the brake pedal.
Reverse slowly and use the hand control.
Reverse slowly and press the brake pedal.
Move forward slowly and use the hand control.

questions.correctAnswerText: Move forward slowly and use the hand control.
questions.explanation: Check that air pressure is normal and release the parking brake. Then move forward slowly and use the hand control to apply the brakes. You should feel the trailer brakes working.

questions.question: Are fully-loaded rigs more or less likely to roll over?

options.text: Less likely to roll over than empty rigs.
More likely to roll over than empty rigs.
Just as likely to roll over as empty rigs.

questions.correctAnswerText: More likely to roll over than empty rigs.
questions.explanation: Fully-loaded rigs have a higher center of gravity because of the cargo weight. They are 10 times more likely to roll over in a crash than empty rigs.

questions.question: If a trailer begins to skid, what should the driver do?
questions.correctAnswerText: Release the brakes.
questions.explanation: Release the brakes so the wheels can regain traction. Once the wheels grip the road again, the trailer will straighten out and follow the tractor.

questions.question: How should cargo be placed to prevent a rollover?

options.text: As high as possible inside the trailer.
As low as possible inside the trailer.
On the passenger side of the trailer.
On the driver's side of the trailer.

questions.correctAnswerText: As low as possible inside the trailer.
questions.explanation: Keep cargo weight as low as possible to reduce rollover risk. Do not place cargo primarily on one side, as this can cause the trailer to lean and increase rollover risk.

questions.question: What is the easiest way to know your trailer is skidding?

options.text: Look in your mirrors to see if the trailer left the lane.
Release the brake pedal and push it again.
Watch for a jackknife warning light on the control panel.

questions.correctAnswerText: Look in your mirrors to see if the trailer left the lane.
questions.explanation: The easiest way to spot a trailer skid is to use your mirrors. When you brake hard, check your mirrors to make sure your trailer is still in the correct position.

questions.question: When driving slower than 40 mph, keep at least ____ of following distance for every 10 feet of your vehicle.
questions.correctAnswerText: One second
questions.explanation: Below 40 mph, allow at least one second of following distance for every 10 feet of your vehicle. Use the same formula at faster speeds, then add one extra second. Larger vehicles need more space to stop than smaller ones.

questions.question: When driving a combination rig, your following distance should be:

options.text: Shorter than when driving a single vehicle.
About the same as when driving a single vehicle.
Longer than when driving a single vehicle.

questions.correctAnswerText: Longer than when driving a single vehicle.
questions.explanation: Keep more following distance with a combination rig than with a single vehicle. Combination rigs need longer distances to stop.

questions.question: Trailers with low clearance underneath may be difficult to drive:
questions.correctAnswerText: Over railroad crossings.
questions.explanation: Crossings at railroad-highway intersections are hard to cross with a low-clearance trailer. Low-slung units and single-axle tractors pulling long trailers have special difficulty crossing raised railroad crossings.

questions.question: After you finish a pre-trip inspection, you should:

options.text: Leave the rear shut-off valves open.
Leave the emergency line valve open.

questions.correctAnswerText: Close the emergency line valve.
questions.explanation: Before driving, open the rear emergency line and service line shut-off valves to check for air leaks on all trailers. Close both shut-off valves before you start driving.

questions.question: To reduce the risk of a rollover, you should:

options.text: Load cargo as far forward as possible.
Load cargo as far back as possible.
Load cargo as low as possible.
Stack cargo as high as possible.

questions.correctAnswerText: Load cargo as low as possible.
questions.explanation: Load your cargo as close to the ground as possible to reduce rollover risk. Also take curves and corners slowly to further reduce this risk.

questions.question: The trailer hand valve should be used:

options.text: Often to activate trailer brakes in all driving conditions.
Only to test the trailer brakes.
Only in bad weather when the trailer may skid.
Only if the trailer is carrying a load.

questions.correctAnswerText: Only to test the trailer brakes.
questions.explanation: Use the trailer hand valve only to test the trailer brakes. Do not use it while driving because it can cause the trailer to skid.

questions.question: When you connect glad hands, the seals should be pressed together at an angle of:
questions.correctAnswerText: 90 degrees.
questions.explanation: Connect the correct glad hands. The seals should be pressed together at a 90-degree angle when coupled.

questions.question: When driving a bobtail tractor, you should know that:

options.text: Bobtails cannot drive as fast as tractors with trailers.
Bobtails are harder to stop than tractors with trailers.
Bobtails are illegal in most states.

questions.correctAnswerText: Bobtails are harder to stop than tractors with trailers.
questions.explanation: A bobtail tractor has no trailer attached. When driving a bobtail, stopping is difficult and takes a longer distance than stopping a tractor with a loaded trailer.

questions.question: To prevent a trailer from rolling over, you should:

options.text: Speed up when nearing a corner.
Drive faster than the speed limit on on-ramps.

questions.correctAnswerText: Drive slowly around corners.
questions.explanation: To reduce rollover risk when driving a combination vehicle, keep cargo weight as low as possible and drive slowly around turns.
